kinship

/KIN-ship/ — rhymes with friendship · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Kinship is a feeling of closeness and connection with someone, as though they were family, or the actual bond between relatives.

Growing up on farms, the two students felt an instant kinship.

Example

Though the two writers had never met before, they discovered an instant kinship over their shared passion for mystery novels.

Kinship is more precise than 'connection' or 'friendship' here because it captures both the depth (like family) and the immediacy of feeling bonded despite being strangers.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rapport: Rapport is the easy, trusting connection two people fall into: conversation flows, jokes land, silences feel comfortable. It describes how smoothly you get along. Kinship runs deeper than getting along — it is the sense that someone belongs with you like family, whether or not the conversation is easy.

camaraderie: Camaraderie is the friendly trust and good humor that grows among members of a group — teammates, castmates, coworkers — while they share an activity. It belongs to the group. Kinship is a deeper, person-to-person bond: the feeling that this particular person is like family to you.

solidarity: Solidarity is the loyalty people show one another because they share a cause or a struggle — striking workers, teammates under pressure. It binds a group around a purpose. Kinship needs no cause: it is a family-like closeness felt person to person, and it outlasts any single fight.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

alienation: feeling cut off from other people

estrangement: the loss of a once-close bond

Where it sits · how deep the bond runs

acquaintance → affinity → kinship → brotherhood

acquaintance vs. kinship: Acquaintance is the weakest: an acquaintance is merely someone you know, while kinship is a deep sense that someone belongs with you like family.

affinity vs. kinship: Affinity is stronger than acquaintance but weaker than kinship — affinity is a natural liking or pull toward someone, while kinship feels like an actual family bond.

brotherhood vs. kinship: Brotherhood is stronger even than kinship: kinship is the feeling of being like family, while brotherhood declares a total, sworn family loyalty among its members.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — kin: family, race (Old English)

Suffix — -ship: state or condition of (Old English)

Put it together: Kin ('family') + -ship ('state or condition of') literally means 'the condition of being family' — kinship is that family bond, or the feeling of closeness that makes someone feel like family.

Use the root in a new word: kindred: The two poets became kindred spirits the day they discovered they owned the same battered favorite book.

Word Choice

neutral / literary

Kinship describes a deep emotional bond like family, not just friendship or agreement. Use it when two people feel genuinely connected at a profound level, often instantly despite being new to each other. For casual friendship, 'connection' is simpler; for shared circumstances, 'camaraderie' is more precise.
